analysis.one_liner: Lets cities, towns, public-private partnerships, and cooperatives build broadband even where states have banned it.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2021 with 7 senators behind it, but the Senate Commerce Committee never acted on it and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: More than a dozen states have laws that stop local governments, public-private partnerships, or cooperatives from offering their own broadband service, usually to protect the big cable and phone companies from public competition. This bill would wipe out those state bans nationwide, while requiring any public network to apply its own local rules fairly to the private companies it competes with. It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never came back out.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of rural areas and low-income neighborhoods that big providers have left unserved or overpriced, because their cities, counties, electric co-ops, or tribal entities could build or partner on broadband even in states that currently forbid it. Taxpayers in those communities would gain a competitive alternative to the incumbent cable and telephone companies.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Telecommunications Act to prohibit any state law or regulation that prohibits a public provider, public-private partnership, or cooperative from providing advanced telecommunications capability, i.e. broadband.

It includes safeguards for private competitors: a public provider must apply its ordinances and rules without discriminating in favor of itself, and a savings clause keeps all ordinary federal and state telecom regulations applying to public networks.
The bill defines 'state or local entity' to include Indian Tribes, so tribal governments could build broadband even where state law currently blocks them.

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent cable and telephone companies would face new public and cooperative competitors in markets where state law has shielded them, and public networks would be financed by the state or local governments that build them, meaning taxpayers bear the risk if a project underperforms.
analysis.who_pays_short: Cable and telephone incumbents; local taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Public broadband networks are financed by local governments, so a failed or overspent project would land on local taxpayers; the bill opens this door in every state without imposing its own financing tests.

The antidiscrimination clause limits what cities can do to favor their own networks over private competitors, a constraint that public-network advocates accepted to blunt industry objections to the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's public benefit is potentially large: where private companies will not build, or charge monopoly prices, a municipal or cooperative alternative can force competition and extend service to unserved areas. The main cost is that local taxpayers finance these projects and bear the risk when they underperform, and the bill's safeguards modestly constrain public networks. The tradeoff is a reasonable one, but it was never tested because the bill never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never held a markup or vote, so it died when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the Community Broadband Act on April 29, 2021, joined by Sens. Markey, King, Wyden, Blumenthal, Sanders, and Gillibrand.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
The bill's only recorded actions are the introduction and the committee referral; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote followed before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill would have barred states from prohibiting public, public-private partnership, or cooperative broadband providers, directly overriding the state-level restrictions that exist in many states.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The incumbent cable and telephone companies are better off: the state laws that shield them from public competition remain on the books, and no congressional route to overriding them advanced. Communities that wanted to build their own networks are no better off than before.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Community Broadband Act of 2021 to override state bans on public, partnership, and cooperative broadband.

for.name: Sens. Markey, King, Wyden, Blumenthal, Sanders, and Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; four Senate Democrats and both Senate independents backed it.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee; after the April 2021 referral, no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Large cable and telephone companies
against.what_they_did: The industry has long backed the state laws this bill would override and opposed efforts to allow municipal broadband competition.

sides.party_line_note: All seven original sponsors were Democrats or independents; no Senate Republican cosponsored the bill, though Sen. Angus King, an independent, joined it.

industries.industry: Cable and telephone broadband incumbents (Comcast, Charter, AT&T, Verizon and similar)
industries.note: The bill would let public and cooperative networks compete directly in markets these companies hold, often as the only provider, ending the state-law shield against that competition. Their gain from the bill dying is the continuation of monopoly or duopoly pricing in unserved areas.

industries.industry: Municipal utilities, electric cooperatives, and community broadband networks
industries.note: The bill's core purpose is to let these entities build and sell broadband in states that currently prohibit them. Where they succeed, residents get another provider option and often lower prices.

Cities and counties gain a new tool to address connectivity gaps, but they finance the networks, so residents bear the risk of projects that underperform. The bill's antidiscrimination clause also limits how much a city can favor its own network.
